correctness.rationale: For each graph, the explicitly defined basis table is associative since every triple product in the radical vanishes, and the quotient by the radical is the field. Squaring a general radical element yields exactly the independent basis coefficients c_i c_j for graph edges; no cancellation is possible even in characteristic two. The edge ideal is squarefree and radical. Its minimal coordinate primes, support decomposition, Hilbert-series monomial enumeration, and finite-field counts give the asserted consequences. The full-scheme reduction follows because its scalar coordinate has square zero in the defining ideal. The #P-hardness is a polynomial-time one-call Turing reduction from counting graph independent sets, using the factor 2^m. The actual standalone script verifies associativity and point counts on 82 finite instances; finite tests are only supportive. In algebraically closed characteristic two, the commutative squaring coordinate polynomials are squares of linear forms, so their radical ideal is generated by linear forms; any graph containing an edge has distinct maximal independent-set components, proving the commutative boundary.

value.rationale: The theorem realizes every finite graph independence complex as the natural reduced square-zero geometry of a short local associative algebra, uniformly including characteristic two where symmetric cross-term cancellation prevents the naïve commutative construction. Consequently arbitrary graph component arrangements, non-equidimensional examples, independence-polynomial point counts, and #P-hard finite-field enumeration arise already with cube-zero radical. This is a structurally motivated general correspondence and complexity transfer, not an arbitrary isolated numerical computation. The commutative-versus-noncommutative obstruction in characteristic two proves the realization is not merely a redundant commutative embedding.
